Seven people missing after fire on vessel in Black Sea off Romania
Just as the leaders sit down at the big table in Brussels, Romania has said that seven people are still missing after a fire on a vessel in Romanian territorial waters of the Black Sea.
An aerial footage shows San Marino-flagged tanker wine trader ship that caught fire in Romanian territorial waters. Photograph: Romanian Interior Ministry/Reuters
Suspected Russian drones have hit several ships off Romania and neighbouring Bulgaria since last week in a spillover from the Ukraine war, AFP reported.
Romanian authorities did not say whether a drone caused the fire on the vessel, named as the Wine Trader, which reported a blaze at around 7am, approximately 13 nautical miles southeast of the Romanian city of Sulina.
“Whether it was struck by a drone or not, an investigation is currently underway,” defence minister Radu Miruță told the Digi24 television channel.
The Romanian Naval Authority said in a statement there were 12 people on board the vessel, AFP reported.
Eight crew were initially reported as missing.
“Five of the sailors on board the Wine Trader have been rescued, a further seven people are still missing,” the Naval Authority said in an update.Share
EU will voice dismay and 'regret' over the US diesel deal with RussiaJennifer Rankin
EU leaders will voice dismay over Donald Trump’s decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel.
European Council summit Photograph: dts News Agency Germany Michael Kappeler Pool/Shutterstock
“The European Council regrets the United States’ decision to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel,” states a draft statement seen by the Guardian to be issued by the 27 leaders when the two-day summit concludes on Friday.
Other leaders, such as Sweden’s Ulf Kristersson, were blunter in their assessment of the deal (9.36).
But EU leaders tread a fine line between their obvious dislike of Trump’s actions towards Russia and dependence on US military support.
That balancing act was epitomised by comments from Estonia’s prime minister, Kristen Michal.
He recalled that the US was one of three Nato nuclear-armed partners supporting his country and described the US as “strong allies” (the others are the UK and France).
He referenced Nato’s help when Estonia faced hybrid attacks and other threats, such as the cutting of cables, Russian fighter jet incursions and drones.
“This kind of help came from Nato and we still have Nato ships on the sea guarding our critical infrastructure. So, [based] on that I must say that Nato is working well and the US is a partner in Nato. And Trump has assured us and everybody else last time in Ankara that he is following Nato and also Article 5 [on collective defence]. So we rely on them – and also sometimes even good friends need a reminder what is right.”
Estonia’s prime minister Kristen Michal answers journalists’ questions upon his arrival for a European Union summit at the EU headquarters in Brussels. Photograph: Nicolas Tucat/AFP/Getty ImagesShare
We should put pressure on Russia, not Ukraine, EU's foreign policy chief says
EU’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas acknowledged that the EU and the US had “definitely different approach to this war,” as she said Europeans believe “we should squeeze Russia, not Ukraine, to surrender and end this war.”
European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas speaks with the media as she arrives for the EU summit at the European Council building in Brussels. Photograph: Harry Nakos/AP
Responding to the US diesel deal with Russia, she said:
“The majority of Russia’s funding for the war comes from oil revenues. Clearly, Ukraine wants this war to stop, and that’s why … cutting off the funding for the war is the way to do it.
We see that we should squeeze … Russia, not Ukraine, to surrender to end this war.”
She added that the EU has adopted a new round of sanction listings earlier this week, as “this is the only way to put pressure on Russia.”
She also said that it’s important to send a clear message to Russia that “all these things they are interested in – [unfreezing] frozen assets, lifting the sanctions – are actually up to Europeans to decide.”
“And these things are not given for free for them,” she said.Share
Germany's Merz calls for stronger support for Ukraine, but warns of 'very, very difficult' budget talks
Germany’s Friedrich Merz also focused on the budget talks, saying they remain “very, very difficult” and expecting them to run well into December.
German chancellor Friedrich Merz speaks to the media as he arrives for a European Council summit in Brussels, Belgium. Photograph: Olivier Matthys/EPA
On Ukraine, he warned that “we are witnessing an increasingly ruthless wave of attacks by Russia,” and said that “we must do everything possible to support Ukraine not just through the winter, but into next year as well.”
“It remains my firm conviction that we are not merely defending Ukraine’s territorial integrity; we are defending the political order of Europe, which is being subjected to intense pressure by Russia in every respect.”
Hungary’s Péter Magyar focused on other issues in his doorstep statement, particularly on migration and the next EU budget.
Hungarian prime minister Péter Magyar arrives for a European Council summit in Brussels, Belgium. Photograph: Olivier Matthys/EPA
But he welcomed the much-awaited law reform in Ukraine that could resolve a longstanding dispute over the rights of the Hungarian minority in western Ukraine, which until now threatened to bloc Kyiv’s accession path.‘He cares about Hungarians’: the small Ukrainian town divided over Orbán
Magyar will hold a one-on-one with Ukraine’s Zelenskyy tomorrow, his first since ousting Viktor Orbán and coming into power earlier this year.Share
Ireland's Martin urges Europe to 're-engage' with US, but also calls for 'practical' support for Ukraine with EU accession prospects
Ireland’s Micheál Martin urged Europe to “re-engage” with the US and figure out the best way forward, despite tensions over Ukraine.
“We have had moments in the past when there were challenges and difficulties in respect of this, and it was retrieved by good outreach and engagement from Europe with the US, and I have no doubt that will continue.”
Irish taoiseach Micheal Martin arrives for a European Council summit in Brussels, Belgium. Photograph: Olivier Matthys/EPA
But he said the focus should also be on what the EU can do itself, and that’s primarily to do with advancing Ukraine’s accession process to the bloc.
“I would say to my colleagues across Europe that now is the time to be ambitious over the next number of months to open all clusters in respect of Ukraine and Moldova. The people of Ukraine need that as a very strong signal, given the extraordinary pressure they are under from the Russian attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure.”
He said “the most fundamental thing we can do in Europe now is to recommit to opening all clusters in respect of Ukraine’s application.” “That would send a powerful signal to the people of Ukraine that Europe is really progressing its pathway to accession,” he said.
The recent attacks are “appalling and horrific, and it illustrates that Putin is not interested in peace.”
“That’s why we must manifest our support for Ukraine in the practical ways … and certainly the membership agenda is one of those.”Share
'We very much regret this agreement on diesel,' Sweden's Kristersson says
Sweden’s Ulf Kristersson also offered his backing for Ukraine, as he criticised Donald Trump’s diesel deal with Russia.
“We very much regret this agreement on diesel. It’s obviously not a very big part, but still, it’s in the wrong direction. And every step now to help the Russians to increase their the financing of the war is a bad sign.
So we very much stick to Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s view on this.”
This 'senseless war of aggression' only continues because of Putin, Dutch PM says
EU leaders are now arriving for the European Council summit in Brussels and understandably they get asked about the latest situation in Ukraine.
Dutch prime minister Rob Jetten speaks with the media as he arrives for the EU summit at the European Council building in Brussels. Photograph: Harry Nakos/AP
Dutch PM Rob Jetten offered his strong backing for Ukraine and president Volodymyr Zelenskyy, saying “there is only one reason why this senseless war of aggression is continuing, and that’s because Putin chooses to do so.”
“He is the one that can end this war by starting negotiations for just and lasting peace. And as long as he doesn’t, the Ukrainians will have to defend themselves and defend European values, and we stand shoulder to shoulder with the Ukrainians.”
He urged other leaders “to do more financially, militarily, and non-militarily, because a lot of European countries are lagging behind in the support for Ukraine.”
“So let’s step up our game and make sure that they can win this senseless war.”
Starlink satellite restrictions highlight Europe's dependency on US technology
As Ukraine reported problems with Starlink satellite internet terminals and US data that warns of Russian ballistic missile attacks, Kyiv also faced the harsh reality that its European allies cannot offer ⁠any ready-made alternatives, Reuters reported.
A Starlink satellite internet system is set up near the frontline town of Bakhmut amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, Donetsk region. Photograph: Lisi Niesner/Reuters
European countries have voiced strong support for Ukraine and Zelenskyy. But the problems with vital data highlighted that Ukraine and Europe depend heavily ‌on US systems for both low-orbit satellite communications – provided by SpaceX via Starlink – and space-based infrared sensing that feeds into early-warning systems.
A US satellite constellation called the Space-Based Infrared System provides early missile warnings.
As for Starlink, Europe does not have a ready-made alternative that Ukrainian soldiers could attach to their drones, although European governments and companies are working on long-term options.
Shares in European satellite operator Eutelsat soared on Wednesday following news of Ukraine’s difficulties with Starshield, fuelled by ‌investor bets that European providers could benefit from growing strains between Washington and Kyiv.Share
Morning opening: Musk suggests US government was behind Starlink restrictions
Billionaire tech mogul Elon Musk has suggested that the US government could be behind the decision to restrict the speed of SpaceX’s satellite-technology used by Ukraine’s military.What is Starshield, SpaceX’s military-grade Starlink system, and how will its restriction affect Ukraine?
In a post of X, he appeared to suggest the Trump administration was behind the move, which Ukraine says restricts its ability to use key defensive weapons.In Ukraine, civilian casualties were already rising. Restrictions on Starlink will only worsen the death toll
A Ukrainian serviceman of 47th brigade prepares a Starlink satellite internet systems at his positions at a front line. Photograph: Reuters
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.
Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.”
In further posts overnight, reacting to Zelenskyy’s comments on his relationship with Donald Trump, Musk went further and appeared to suggest Zelenskyy should leave the post, saying it’s “time to go.”
In a TV interview with Piers Morgan, Zelenskyy said he felt “betrayed” by Trump’s decisions and worried about “losing a strong partner,” playing a critical role across Ukraine’s defence.Volodymyr Zelenskyy feels ‘betrayed’ by Donald Trump over Starlink access
For what it’s worth, Trump denied that his administration had cut intelligence sharing on Tuesday, but Zelenskyy said in an interview with US broadcaster NPR, aired on Wednesday, that military advisers had received threats from the US that intelligence sharing could be limited in the future.
The issue is likely to come up again today and tomorrow as EU leaders meet in Brussels for key political talks on the future.
With today’s discussions focused on the bloc’s internal matters, including the EU’s next budget, Ukraine is expected to come up on Friday when Zelenskyy joins other leaders in Brussels. But the ongoing crisis in Ukraine’s relations with the US risks overshadowing the entire meeting.

EU has to act on energy prices to prevent people from turning to populists and extremists, EU commissioner warnsJennifer Rankin
Europe has to take action to curb soaring oil and gas prices to prevent people from turning to populists and extremists, a senior EU official has said.
European Commissioner for Energy Dan Jørgensen Photograph: Omar Havana/Reuters
Dan Jørgensen, the European commissioner for energy and housing policy, said EU governments could choose actions to make fossil fuels cheaper as long as they were “targeted” and “temporary” so as not to derail the continent from its goal to tackle the climate crisis by drastically cutting carbon emissions.
Earlier this week European gas prices hit their highest level since the winter of 2022, when consumers faced rising prices in the wake of supply disruption following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Meanwhile global oil prices have surged to $92 a barrel, an increase of $20 a barrel since March with even bigger price increases in some product markets, the International Energy Agency reported this week
Speaking to the Guardian and other European newspapers, Jørgensen said the EU was approaching a “tough” winter for citizens and business with “no signs that the situation in the Middle East is improving”.
A Circle-K petrol station in downtown of Riga, Latvia. Photograph: Wojtek Radwański/AFP/Getty Images
Since the US and Israel launched the war on Iran that unleashed spiralling oil and gas prices, the EU had spent an extra €110bn (£93bn) paying for energy it would not have spent if supplies had remained stable, according to EU estimates.
Faced with that situation governments and the EU had to take action to help people heat their homes and put petrol in their cars, the commissioner said, even if that meant favouring fossil fuels in the short-term.
Jørgensen, a former Danish climate and energy minister, pointed out that even in an average year nearly 50m people in Europe struggle to heat their homes.
“If we do not tackle what people see as their most fundamental problems every day… if they do not have the ability to pay their bills at the end of the month, there’s a risk that they will listen to populists and extremists.”
He said governments could subsidise fossil fuels if necessary, “but it needs to be targeted and it needs to be temporary.”
He was speaking on Wednesday when the European Commission proposed a one-year delay to the EU’s methane ⁠emissions rules for oil and gas imports under pressure from the US, but also France. The rules, due to ⁠take effect on January ⁠1, 2027, would have required foreign oil and gas suppliers to the EU to monitor and report methane, a super-polluting greenhouse gas.
Earlier this year the European Commission proposed a major overhaul of the EU’s emissions trading system, the EU’s flagship policy to cut polluting emissions. Green groups fear the plans will weaken what they see as the EU’s most effective tool in fighting planet-heating gases.
But many member states are looking for more, including scrapping an extension of the ETS to housing and transport.
EU leaders, who discussed fuel prices on Thursday, are expected to call for the EU executive “to examine and put forward as needed further measures to address soaring energy prices in the short term” according to a draft of their summit conclusions.Share

Serbian ruler’s secret role in ‘illegal’ effort to help Trump businessTom Burgis
Meanwhile, Serbia’s authoritarian ruler personally intervened to advance an allegedly illegal scheme to hand over a protected site in Belgrade for a Trump tower, the Guardian can reveal.
Jared Kushner visiting Serbian president Aleksandar Vucic. Photograph: Instagram/Aleksandar Vucic
Aleksandar Vučić summoned officials to a meeting at his presidential offices about the project, which has culminated in a landmark indictment of senior figures from his regime on charges of abuse of public office.
The criminal case is believed to be the first resulting from the Trumps’ global moneymaking campaign, described by critics as a “pay to play” arrangement where everything from sanctions relief to cutting-edge chips is available to those who enrich the first family and their associates.
The alleged scheme to override the protected status of a historic building in the Serbian capital looms over an election scheduled for 25 October, when Vučić will seek to extend his 12 years in power in the face of a mass protest movement spurred by government corruption.
Serbian students and Belgrade residents hold a banner reading ‘We won’t give up the General Staff building’ in Belgrade in November 2025. Photograph: Andrej Isaković/AFP/Getty Images
A nationalist former propaganda chief under Slobodan Milošević, Vučić hosted the US president’s son Donald Trump Jr and son-in-law Jared Kushner in Belgrade as they developed plans for a $500m hotel and residential tower to add to their global property portfolios.
After the abuse of power charges were brought last December, Kushner’s company announced the project would not proceed “at this time”. Vučić threatened reprisals, calling the prosecutors “corrupt gangs” who “fabricated cases”.
“We have lost an exceptional investment,” the Serbian president said. “I will personally ensure that everyone who participated in causing this damage is held accountable.”
Vučić’s culture minister is among those charged with abuse of power. But a Guardian investigation, drawing on interviews and leaked documents, reveals that the Serbian president himself led the initial meeting where the alleged scheme was discussed. This crucial meeting is not mentioned in the indictment, raising questions about what information the prosecutors are holding back and why.
Representatives of the Trumps and Kushner said they had no part in the removal of the building’s protected status and that it would be “false” to say the Belgrade project was part of a “pay to play” scheme.
Vučić did not respond to requests for comment. His decision to call a snap election means that a hearing at which witnesses might reveal details of his involvement will not take place until after the vote.Revealed: Serbian ruler’s secret role in ‘illegal’ effort to help Trump business
Russia attempting to destabilise societies across Nato, Romania's Dan says after drone incidents
Meanwhile, Romania’s Nicușor Dan has warned that Russia seeks to “destabilise societies – not just in Romania and Bulgaria, but across European nations, particularly those on the Eastern Flank,” as he responded to overnight drone attacks on ships in Romanian territorial waters of the Black Sea (12:03).
Romania’s president Nicușor Dan briefing the media on the margins of the European Council summit in Brussels, Belgium. Photograph: Romanian presidential office YouTube channel
Briefing the media in Brussels after his meeting with Nato’s Mark Rutte and Bulgaria’s Rumen Radev (13:01, 14:31), Dan said they discussed the recent incidents in Romania and Bulgaria, and that he believed there was “a need for equipment suited to this new type of challenge.”
He said that’s what happened when Romania was affected by stray drones coming into its territory. “You will recall that … we turned to the allies, some military equipment arrived and the situation stabilised.”
“Clearly, Russia is attempting to destabilise societies – not just in Romania and Bulgaria, but across European nations, particularly those on the Eastern Flank – and to erode support for Ukraine.
Our response is to continue supporting Ukraine, as this is a matter of international law and a matter concerning Romania’s own security.”
However, he did not offer more details about the incidents, saying the investigation was ongoing.Share
Zelenskyy to meet with Nato's Rutte, several national leaders as he lands in Brussels for EU summit
The Ukrainian president also confirmed he’s now in Brussels, where he is expected to meet with Nato’s Mark Rutte later today, and join the European Council tomorrow.
He will also hold bilateral talks with Belgium’s de Wever (no doubt on frozen assets), Denmark’s Frederiksen, France’s Macron and Poland’s Tusk.
“Tomorrow, meetings are planned with the presidents of the European Council and the European Commission, as well as the prime ministers of Hungary, Finland, and Sweden.
All of us in Europe want this war to end. And for that to happen, strong signals are needed – more real pressure on Russia and more defence support for Ukraine. It is especially important now to act together to protect lives.”
Zelenskyy claims Ukraine destroyed four Russian planes by striking airfield
A Ukrainian missile strike destroyed four fighter jets at an airfield in western Russia overnight, Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said in a social media post.
The Ukraine president said:
Last night, Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck an airfield in the Voronezh region. Four Su-34 aircraft were destroyed and two more Su-34s were hit. Our Long Neptune missile was used to strike the target.
The claim has not been independently verified, and there has been no immediate comment from Russia’s defence ministry. The Voronezh region borders Ukraine.Share

My responsibility is to listen, address legitimate concerns and keep Albania moving forward. The alternative would be a betrayal of the Albanians who gave me a strong mandate to complete negotiations on EU membership.

EU leaders heading for mighty clash over EU's next long-term budget - snap analysisJennifer Rankin
One other thing that is clear from this morning’s doorstep statements: leaders are heading for a mighty clash over the EU’s next long-term budget.
Inside the European Council’s meeting room. Photograph: dts News Agency Germany Michael Kappeler Pool/Shutterstock
Agreeing the EU seven-year budget is always a fraught negotiating exercise, which pits a group of “frugals”, such as Germany, Sweden, the Netherlands, who oppose a bigger budget, against a larger group in southern and eastern Europe, who want to maintain the EU’s traditional spending on agriculture and regional funding.
European Council president António Costa wanted a deal by the end of the year to ensure that the next long-term budget (2028-35) would be ready on time – and avoid getting caught in the crossfire of major elections next year in France, Poland and Italy.
European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen and European Council president António Costa talk on the day of the European Union leaders’ summit in Brussels, Belgium. Photograph: Yves Herman/Reuters
That timing is in doubt, as the EU’s frugals (who prefer to be called “modernisers”) reiterated this morning they are in no hurry.
Sweden’s prime minister Ulf Kristersson said he expected tense talks today.
“We are not reaching agreement this month, not next month. I don’t know even if it’s possible to reach an agreement before the end of the year. I think we are not in a hurry, honestly. We need to have a budget that could combine the modernisation, the resources for Ukraine and of course the traditional things as well. But all the titles [areas of spending] need to be decreased to be able to reach an agreement.”
Friedrich Merz said he expected the “very, very difficult” talks to run into December (11:05) but privately Germany has made it clear it is ready to see the talks go into next year unless there are massive cuts to the current proposal.
In the other camp is Spain’s Pedro Sánchez, who described the current proposal as “insufficient” to face the bloc’s challenges, adding that his government would fight to expand it. But with Spain due to hold elections in November, the Socialist leader may not be around to make that argument.
The latest draft summit conclusions call for only a “timely agreement” rather than setting a deadline “by the end of the year”, as in an earlier version.
The European Commission’s €2tn (£1.7tn) budget proposal, which aims to increase spending on defence, border security and research, has already been trimmed by €140bn by Ireland, who as holders of the rotating presidency were tasked with finding a common ground by October.
But almost nobody is happy.
The frugal camp thinks the cuts, which target defence and research, are in the wrong places, while the self-styled “friends of cohesion” think there is too much scrimping on the EU’s traditional priorities, such as regional development funds.
France, which does not belong in either camp, but faces acute budget pressures, wants to see the EU agree to new common taxes in order to fund a budget that allows increased spending on new priorities such as defence and maintain the traditional ones, such as farm subsidies.
While the Commission has floated EU taxes on big companies, tobacco and e-waste, member states cannot agree on any of the options.
And the whole budget has to be agreed … by unanimity.Share

Swedish parliament rejects Andersson's PM candidacy
A quick update from Sweden, where the country’s parliament rejected Social Democrats leader Magdalena Andersson’s candidacy to form a single-party minority government.
Swedish Social Democratic party leader Magdalena Andersson speaks during a press conference at the Riksdag, the Swedish parliament, in Stockholm, Sweden. Photograph: Jonas Ekstromer/EPA
Only 99 lawmakers voted in favour, with 248 against. Two people were absent.
The vote, forced by the parliament’s speaker Andreas Norlén, was widely expected to fail, but is intended to put more pressure on parties as they continue discussions on who could form the next government.
Four centre-left opposition parties, which have all said they favour ‌Andersson as prime minister, won last month a majority of seats in Sweden’s parliament, ⁠the Riksdag, but ​do not ​agree on ​who should be ​part ‌of ​a ​new government.
Norlén will now have to appoint a new candidate to hold further exploratory talks on the new government.Share
'Sanctions must not be lifted,' Zelenskyy says, as he says Russia's attacks come 'in response to signals from US'
Oh, and we have just heard from Zelenskyy again, doubling down on his criticism of Russia and attributing its latest attacks to “signals from the US.”
Responding to a “horrific” drone attack on a supermarket in Odesa, he said:
“Russia continues its bloody terror. The store was partially destroyed, and cars were damaged. Three people were injured. All necessary emergency services are working at the scene and providing assistance to those affected. It is important that our partners help us defend against this. Residential buildings, stores, energy and other critical infrastructure are under attack virtually nonstop. Not a single hour of peace.”
“What is happening is Russia’s pointed response to the signals it is receiving from America. Unfortunately, there are dangerous signals about the possibility of further sanctions relief. These sanctions were imposed by the world, by America, Europe, and our partners in response to Russia’s aggression against Ukraine and its war against us. Nothing has changed. The war has not stopped. The sanctions must not be lifted. Russia must end the slaughter it itself started and has continued for 1,695 days now. More money to fund the killing will not help bring this about. Strength is what is needed, and America is stronger than Russian terror.”
US effort to get Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire collapsesAndrew Roth
The White House’s unilateral effort to negotiate an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine has collapsed as Moscow sent a record swarm of drones overnight to attack infrastructure in central Ukraine and Kyiv appeared to resume strikes on Russian oil refineries – despite warnings from Donald Trump.
A man stands at the site of his parents' private house, destroyed during a Russian air strike, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, on the outskirts of Dnipro, Ukraine. Photograph: Reuters
Moscow accused Ukraine of launching its first strike against a Russian oil refinery in the Ryazan region since Trump abruptly declared an “energy ceasefire” that neither Russia nor Ukraine said they had agreed to. Trump has demanded that Volodymyr Zelenskyy stop attacking Russian oil refineries, claiming that it was the cause of a global rise in the price of diesel fuel.
Zelenskyy said on Wednesday that he would resume strikes on Russian oil refineries after halting those attacks to show that Ukraine was ready for peace talks. “The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done,” he told the Financial Times. He also attacked the gap in US intelligence sharing as “dangerous”.
Images from Ryazan showed flames at the refinery, which regional officials said had been targeted by 69 drones and four Flamingo cruise missiles. Debris from a drone struck by anti-aircraft fire had hit the refinery and sparked the fire, the ministry claimed.
In Ukraine, more than 360 Russian drones targeted Kirovohrad, a central region that has been hit less hard than others closer to Russia, in attacks that killed three and injured six.
“The enemy deliberately hit critical infrastructure, transport enterprises, logistics ⁠facilities and residential homes,” the regional governor, Andriy Raikovych, said in a statement.
Zelenskyy said Russia had attacked Ukraine with more than 850 Shahed drones at a time when the speed of Ukraine’s defensive capabilities was being “artificially restricted”, a reference to the sudden limitations on Ukraine’s use of the Starlink and Starshield mobile internet terminals.US effort to get Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire collapses
'We need honesty from our partners about this war,' Zelenskyy says
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy offered an update on last night’s Russian attacks on Ukraine.
“Emergency services are still providing assistance in dozens of our cities and communities. Repair crews and rescuers are working to deal with the aftermath of Russian attacks. For practically all of yesterday and throughout last night, a massive shahed attack was under way. The drones kept coming in waves, and there was not a single hour when our skies were clear of them.”
He said “more than 850” drones were sent against Ukraine, “at a time when the speed of our defence capabilities is being artificially restricted.”
“It is obvious that Russia deliberately chose to escalate its attacks after receiving sanctions relief and seeing attempts to pressure Ukraine. Russia exploits every such opportunity and must be held accountable for what it does. Strong decisions are needed to end this war. Ukraine needs steady support, above all in defending our skies.
We need HONESTY from our partners about this war: It is important that everyone in America stand not with the aggressor, but with our efforts to protect lives, end this war, and guarantee security.”
